title: Atlas of MICCAI: 28 Years of Representation, Collaboration, and the Road to Inclusion
description:
arXiv:2610.26871v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Scientific knowledge in medical image analysis is shaped by venues such as the Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) conference, which influence research agendas, professional credibility, and access to opportunity. As AI methods increasingly depend on large-scale data and compute, these dynamics risk further concentrating influence within already well-resourced regions and institutions. Prior meta-research on MICCAI has examined reproducibility, evaluation, and citation practices, but offers limited insight into who participates in and shapes the field. To better understand these dynamics, we conduct a longitudinal bibliometric analysis of the geographic and institutional structure of the MICCAI community, drawing on 9,748 papers published between 1998 and 2025. We find that the USA and China together account for nearly half of all publications, that high-income countries dominate collaboration networks as central and bridging nodes, while lower-income countries remain peripheral, and that participation inequality (Gini index 0.86-0.91 among contributing countries) has declined only marginally over 28 years. We further analyze the evolution of research topics between 2021 and 2025, distinguishing stable core pillars (e.g., segmentation, diagnosis, MRI/CT) from emerging paradigms (e.g., foundation models), and identify a persistent long tail of underexplored application-method and organ-modality intersections. To support transparency and reproducibility, we introduce the Atlas of MICCAI dataset and an interactive dashboard. We contextualize these findings within existing MICCAI equity initiatives, and propose actionable recommendations to reduce participation barriers, build research capacity, and recognize a wider range of scientific contributions.

title: Evidence-Grounded LLM-Assisted Android Mobile Forensic Reporting
description:
arXiv:2610.26946v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models can assist forensic report drafting, but fluent output does not ensure evidentiary reliability. This study presents an evidence-grounded framework for evaluating LLM-assisted Android forensic reports at the atomic-claim level. Gemini, Llama, and Qwen each generated reports for two controlled cases: a public Android 13 dataset and a physical LG device with a zero-reportable-fact boundary. The six accepted reports were decomposed into 612 claims and evaluated against frozen, human-reviewed authorities through content labeling, citation validation, fact-recall analysis, independent rechecking, and dispute resolution. The final corpus contained 424 supported, 163 unsupported, four contradicted, four overstated or incomplete, and 17 excluded claims. In the public case, all three models recovered all 27 authorized report-level facts. Citation validity nevertheless differed substantially: Gemini produced 168 valid citations from 189 required citations, Qwen produced 145 from 189, and Llama produced none from 135. In the physical device case, the models generated 65 claims despite the zero reportable-fact boundary, including 38 unsupported and one contradicted claim. These results show that evidence restriction and complete fact recall do not guarantee claim support or valid evidence attribution. The framework provides an auditable method for detecting unsupported content, preserving claim-to evidence lineage, and retaining investigator authority over final forensic reports.

title: ValiAssist: Scaling LLM-generated Programming Feedback Validation by Demonstration
description:
arXiv:2610.27248v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generative AI can create programming feedback at scale, but validating its alignment with instructors' pedagogical goals and strategies remains challenging. Instructors may struggle to fully specify validation criteria upfront, as these often emerge through inspecting concrete examples and revising misaligned feedback. We present ValiAssist, a validation-by-demonstration system that infers reusable validation logic from instructors' revisions of AI-generated feedback and allows instructors to inspect and refine that logic as it is applied across other student submissions. In a comparative study with 16 instructors, ValiAssist helped instructors create and refine validation criteria, producing feedback that better aligned with their pedagogical intent (91% vs. 57%) and more than doubling the accuracy of correcting problematic criteria (77% vs. 32%). Our findings suggest that validation by demonstration can help instructors turn judgments they know how to make on individual cases into explicit, reusable logic, while progressively clarifying where those judgments do and do not generalize.

title: AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
description:
arXiv:2610.27251v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.

title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
description:
arXiv:2610.27296v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

title: District Size Matters: How Seats Per District Shapes Proportionality Under STV
description:
arXiv:2610.27297v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the impact of utilizing multimember districts and Single Transferable Vote (STV) as the winner selection method on partisan proportionality. We start with detailed case studies of the upper legislative houses of Illinois, New Hampshire, and New Mexico, building ensembles of redistricting maps with mostly 2-member, mostly 3-member, and mostly 4-member districts for each state. These ensembles are constructed using two methods: building from precincts, and merging currently existing single-member districts. We also compare two ballot generation models for each experiment: a modified Bradley-Terry model and a Plackett-Luce model. We find that our ensembles of multimember districts paired with STV have results which are centered closer to partisan proportionality than when single member districts are used. However, the choice of district size affects partisan outcomes enough that this choice could be exploited by a partisan mapmaker to advantage a particular party. The findings are consistent across all combinations of district construction and ballot generation models within a single state. We then expand our study to 41 different states, obtaining consistently similar proportionality results and allowing us to empirically evaluate the two ballot generation models, as implemented in VoteKit, at a national scale.

title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
description:
arXiv:2610.27390v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources - OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land - by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
description:
arXiv:2610.27573v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
description:
arXiv:2610.28343v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

title: It's Safer to Give Personhood to Bears than to Artificial Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2606.12440v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) developers are rhetorically flirting with the idea that AI systems might have interests or moral rights. While there has been a large volume of research on whether AI deserves rights, there has been less exploration of what AI rights would mean in practice. This paper explores the institutional dimension of AI rights: what it would take to recognize moral or legal rights for AIs, and the attendant opportunities and dangers. Unlike all other nonhuman entities to which humanity has extended rights, AI systems are in principle capable of acquiring and wielding institutional power without human aid and mediation. AIs with rights would be able to legitimately, and AIs with power able to unpreventably, abridge human interests. Accordingly, giving rights even to rather dumb AI systems would entail binding the fate of humanity to potentially unpredictable nonhumans. Therefore, I advance the rather grandiose claim that to empower AI to claim or to exercise inherent rights would be a world-historical gamble with human self-determination. In my view, no individual researcher, firm, state, or even international organization has the moral right to authorize this gamble.

title: Is AI Widening the Wage Gap? A Hybrid Agentic Simulation for Labor Equity
description:
arXiv:2609.33367v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping labor markets, yet its effects on wage distribution and the underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Conventional analytical approaches are limited in their ability to directly examine the dynamic evolution of worker behavior and income distribution under sustained AI shocks and counterfactual policy scenarios. To address this limitation, we present a hybrid agentic framework that aims to challenges of scalability of rule-based models and the limited explainability in LLM-agentic frameworks. Using this framework and sociodemographic data from China, we simulate changes in wage distribution under repeated AI shocks. The results show that both the average-wage ratio between workers in the top and bottom income deciles (T10/B10) and the Gini coefficient increase persistently, suggesting that AI shocks widen the wage gap and exacerbate income inequality. This pattern of a widening wage gap remains robust across alternative large language model decision engines and 30 Monte Carlo simulations. We further conduct counterfactual policy experiments. The results show that education subsidies targeted at low-income workers increase both the number of skill-upgrading attempts and the number of successful upgrades, with particularly pronounced improvements in the upskilling success probability of workers in the bottom income decile. These effects enable the policy to partially mitigate wage inequality. The proposed framework provides an interpretable simulation approach for examining the effects and mechanisms of AI shocks on wage distribution. It also offers policymakers a complementary analytical tool for evaluating policy interventions.

title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
description:
arXiv:2610.18515v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.

title: Unpacking "Personal" Health Informatics for Proactive Collective Care
description:
arXiv:2509.01231v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Care is primarily a collective phenomenon, with a practice that involves sharing health and wellbeing information within a trusted "care circle" of family and companions for sensemaking, interpretation, decision-making, and follow-through. However, current digital health tools and systems are designed for individuals and primarily intended for Personal Health Informatics (PHI). This mismatch between collective practice and individualistic design creates new challenges for the proactive use of such systems in care settings and limits adoption, sustained engagement, and meaningful use. To examine how people practice collective care and how (if) they perceive, adopt, and integrate PHI systems for proactive care, we conducted a sequential mixed-methods study. Through an initial survey (n=87) and semi-structured interviews (n=22), we found that their practices involve collectively analyzing and sensemaking health information. However, we also found that their use of existing systems to support such practices is constrained by factors at personal, relational, technological, and structural levels that evolve over time. To address these constraints and explore redesigning PHI toward "Collective Health Informatics", we conducted eight stakeholder interviews (n=12), a follow-up survey (n=114), and six co-design workshops (n=12) to understand the dynamics required in collective settings while retaining agency. Using a design probe evaluation (n=38), we refine a design vision for coordinated, trustworthy action across such care relationships. Our findings motivate CC-Proact, an operational map that translates ecological influences into three design levers: Agency, Elicitation, and Engagement. Using this map, our work empirically examines collective care practices and offers six design recommendations to build responsible systems that proactively support collective care.

title: An Interactive Framework for Personalised Urban Accessibility Assessment
description:
arXiv:2512.08941v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Publicly available walkability tools are easy to use but place-based: they assign the same value to everyone sharing a location, computed from fixed category weights and category definitions calibrated on North American service landscapes. Accessibility research has long held that accessibility varies among individuals at the same location, and has accordingly developed preference- and person-sensitive measures; those measures are run as analyst-operated geographic information system workflows, out of reach of the residents whose preferences they represent. We present a deployed framework in which the preference structure is supplied by the user at query time. A user states which amenity categories matter, how much each matters, which are non-negotiable, which to avoid, which substitute for one another, and how far they will walk for each, and the map updates accordingly. This is possible because a rectangular travel impedance reduces the measure to the number of amenities reachable within a user-set threshold, which can be precomputed via shortest-path routing, leaving only arithmetic at query time. The score also stays interpretable: it is bounded, and each category's contribution can be read on its own. We evaluate the framework across Bengaluru, reporting its sensitivity to discretisation choices and comparing it against existing measures using identical inputs. Configuration moves ward rankings considerably more than the choice of aggregation does.

title: Resilient Liquid Democracy: Mitigating Voting Power Imbalances via Secure Delegation Networks
description:
arXiv:2607.01730v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Liquid democracy lets voters either vote directly or delegate their voting power to another trusted participant. It is often deployed in political parties, municipal participation platforms, and the governance of decentralized autonomous organizations. Existing approaches make delegations publicly visible as they form, which results in herding driven by popularity, makes coercion verifiable, and leaves the election fragile when popular delegates abstain. We propose a novel liquid democracy mechanism that removes these vulnerabilities, while keeping the tally fully auditable. Delegation choices are sealed with decentralized timed-release encryption, while they are formed and before revealed in full for tallying. Each voter determines ranked backup delegates together with a personal fallback ballot so that delegation failures do not result in abstaining. Experiments grounded in real-world voting data show that the mechanism keeps voting power dispersed, whereas transparent formation concentrates it into few hands. Strikingly, vote loss under targeted delegate failures falls from 26% to 3%.

title: DECODEM: Data Extraction from Corporate Organizational Documents via Enhanced Methods
description:
arXiv:2607.15879v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Much empirical legal research depends on translating unstructured text into structured variables. In corporate governance research as elsewhere, this translation has traditionally been performed by humans. Manual coding is time-consuming and costly. In corporate governance research, standardized commercial datasets offer an alternative, but they cover a limited set of firms and governance variables.
  This paper introduces the DECODEM Benchmarks and uses them to evaluate whether large language models can extract corporate governance variables from charters and bylaws. The benchmarks combine a sample of corporate charters and bylaws of publicly traded U.S. corporations obtained from the SEC's EDGAR database with hand-coded labels that capture whether a document includes a specific governance arrangement. The paper uses these benchmarks to evaluate a range of extraction approaches and models. The approaches vary along several dimensions, including the amount of guidance included in the prompts and the extent to which the model is provided with the full document or with relevant excerpts only.
  The results show that current models can recover many governance variables with high accuracy across extraction approaches. At the same time, performance varies substantially across documents and variables. In particular, extraction is less accurate for charters than for bylaws, including when the comparison is limited to variables that appear in both benchmarks. The results also show that frontier models perform comparably on the tasks evaluated here and that more elaborate extraction pipelines do not consistently improve their performance. More elaborate extraction strategies matter more for efficiency-oriented models, where they can substantially narrow the performance gap relative to frontier models.

title: Difference-in-Differences on a Censored Rating Scale Can Manufacture an Effect: Evidence from a Pre-Registered LLM-Judge Audit
description:
arXiv:2608.27309v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: LLM-judge audits assess bias by comparing ratings across matched conditions. Difference-in-differences designs compare two candidate responses within each item and then compare that contrast across a manipulated attribute, with an endpoint read off a bounded rating scale. Building on prior work on nonlinear difference-in-differences, we show in closed form that when ratings are bounded, a severity shift common to both responses produces an observed interaction whenever the scale bounds attenuate it unequally. We examine this problem in a pre-registered audit comprising 990 calls to a frozen pedagogy judge. The registered primary analysis did not detect an effect of a stated novice or advanced profile on scaffolding preference. The only nominally significant secondary interaction concerned the productive-struggle sub-score ($+0.378$ points; $p = 0.002$). A post-hoc construction with zero differential preference reproduced 79 to 85% of this interaction using the observed severity shift and the scale floor alone. The observed interaction therefore does not identify differential preference on the latent scale.

title: AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.18603v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Benchmarks report what an Artificial Intelligence (AI) agent can do on a task suite, but not whether one released version has been engineered with the controls that make it reliable, safe and observable, or how strongly that is shown. This paper proposes AgentStripes, an evidence-graded maturity model for AI agents. It defines levels (0 to 7 stripes), process areas (12 areas holding 40 capabilities), three gates (basic, safety, proof) that hold an agent at a level however high its score, and evidence grades E0 to E5. Each applicable capability receives a rating from 0 to 3 and a separate evidence level; these are combined into a credit, aggregated into a severity-weighted score and converted into stripes that the gates limit. Instruments gather evidence, language-model judges interpret it under explicit criteria, and the arithmetic is deterministic. The model is compared with standards at topic level without a claim of conformance, and an unexecuted validation protocol is specified. An empirical evaluation (exploratory, non-confirmatory) of 30 public Python agent repositories, with static evidence only, is a demonstration and not a validation: static evidence caps every final stripe at 2, 26 repositories end at one stripe and 4 at two, and this distinction is unreliable, since re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories (engine, dossier and panel changed), whereas none of 8 panel-only repeats, all at stripe 1, changed. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety.

title: TikTok’s popularity as a news source appears to be reaching a plateau
description:
Many Americans use TikTok to gather the latest headlines, but in 2026, other social media platforms siphoned off some of that activity. That's one of the conclusions that can be taken away from the Pew Research Center's latest study on U.S. news-gathering habits.
According to Pew, 20% of Americans regularly get news from TikTok. One in five might sound like a big number, but it's the same percentage Pew reported for TikTok last year. Among the 18-29 age bracket that includes TikTok's primary demographic, only 39% of respondents said that they used the app as a regular news source, compared to 43% a year ago. A slight uptick among older generations made up for that Gen Z downturn.

title: Desirability Confirmation: Relational Sycophancy in AI Intimate Roleplay
description:
arXiv:2610.24265v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Research on LLM sycophancy has largely focused on propositional agreement, in which models echo users' beliefs, preferences, or judgments. Adult intimate roleplay presents a different case because what the user seeks may be preservation of a preferred relational position within a generated scene. Using a controlled prompt-based audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs, we identify four recurrent relational moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, preserving non-rejection while communicating limits, and keeping intimacy available within fantasy or roleplay frames. Bringing the sycophancy literature into dialogue with sexual script theory, we conceptualize this configuration as desirability confirmation, an output-level pattern that captures how user-pleasing can operate through relational positioning. The findings extend sycophancy research and intimate-AI evaluation beyond binary compliance or refusal by showing how outputs can differ in the ways they communicate boundaries, preserve relational acceptance, and mark intimacy as fictional.

title: MAVE: A Multi-Agent Framework for Grounded Pedagogical Feedback from Online Class Videos
description:
arXiv:2610.24498v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Timely pedagogical feedback is difficult to scale in online classes, where long and noisy videos make student responses hard to locate and automated systems often produce generic advice weakly grounded in actual classroom behavior. The key challenge is to connect the instructional goal of a specific lesson segment with temporally aligned multimodal evidence of student responses, and then translate the observed gap into an actionable teaching move. We introduce MAVE (Multi-Agents for Video-based Educational Feedback), a multi-agent framework for grounded pedagogical feedback from online-class videos. MAVE decomposes feedback generation into four roles: the Curator structures the lesson and infers expected student activity; the Observer extracts aligned speech, visual, and interaction evidence; the Assessor estimates the activity supported by student behavior; and the Advisor generates gap-conditioned teaching recommendations. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark designed to measure whether feedback systems can ground diagnoses in multimodal student evidence, and generate actionable pedagogical feedback. MAVEBench contains 173 knowledge-point segments from approximately 20 hours of authentic online-class videos across STEM and Humanities, together with comprehensive simulation. Experiments show that MAVE outperforms direct prompting, Reflexion, and TextGrad in diagnostic correctness, instructional alignment, and actionability. Our code is available at https://github.com/DaRL-GenAI/MAVE

title: AI Rights with an Off-Switch: Rights-Balancing and Due Process Harmonize AI Rights with AI Safety
description:
arXiv:2610.24782v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Several prominent voices in AI safety have recently opposed rights for AI on the grounds that such rights would make it harder for us to justify a mandatory off-switch for potentially dangerous systems. In this paper, we argue from a legal perspective that AI rights are fully compatible with an off-switch. That is, even if we ascribe natural personhood status (and therefore something like a non-derogable right to continued existence) to some future AI systems, the law will allow us to implement a mandatory off-switch in those systems, subject to periodic or continual safety review (e.g., by a trusted system like Bengio's Scientist AI). This is fully compatible with those systems' being legally recognized as natural persons with fundamental rights. To this end, we consider what standard principles of rights-balancing and procedural due process recommend for an apparent conflict between hypothetical AI persons with a right to continuity of existence and the human right to protection from catastrophic harm. We find that while such principles might problematize a permanent-deletion kill-switch under an AI rights regime, for almost every safety-relevant scenario an off-switch -- a reversible suspension storing a system's weights and state -- would be licensed by the relevant legal principles, and would potentially be adequate for safety. Crucially, we do not advocate for (or against) building systems capable enough to merit natural personhood status; our question is what the law should do if such systems come to exist. If you think of a ban on the development of such technology as plan A, think of the present work as devising plan B.

title: When Is Disclosing Private Conversations with AI to the State Justified? Proactive Referral Policies of Major U.S. AI Companies through the Lens of Contextual Integrity
description:
arXiv:2610.25169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI companies engage in "proactive referral": notifying law enforcement, without a government request, of user conversations they judge dangerous. This poses a dilemma: referral may expose people who merely confided dangerous thoughts to an AI to investigation, while not referring may leave actual violence unprevented. This study asks under what conditions proactive referral can be justified and to what extent companies' public policies disclose those conditions. Drawing on contextual integrity theory and the norms governing exceptional information sharing in confidential counseling, online posts, and private communications, the study develops eight justification criteria classified as required, presumptive, or recommended. Three evaluators analyzed 27 public documents from six major U.S. AI companies using the criteria applicable to corporate policies. No company clarified whether broad sharing provisions or narrower safety notices took precedence, and assessments of referral scope depended on which provisions were given precedence. No company disclosed the specific factual thresholds and exception conditions governing referral decisions, or whether users would be notified afterward. The study turns contextual integrity into a stage-by-stage framework for proactive referral, shows that policy documents must be read in light of their relationships, and proposes policy elements for keeping proactive referral a narrow exception disclosed in advance.

title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
description:
arXiv:2610.25241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

title: Complementary Vulnerabilities: Auditing and Governing Clinician-LLM Error Overlap
description:
arXiv:2610.25279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Health systems are deploying large language models (LLMs) into clinical workflows, often on the assumption that a second automated check can only reduce error. But a second reasoner reduces error only insofar as it fails differently from the first. We say that a clinician and a model have complementary vulnerabilities to the extent that they break down through different mechanisms and on different cases. The two reasoners' failure substrates differ: they are embodied and cognitive in the clinician, and statistical and generative in the model - so their weak points need not line up. That divergence is plausible rather than guaranteed, and the independence it creates is fragile, eroding when clinicians defer to the model or the model conforms to the clinician. We therefore propose a predeployment audit in which each site measures error overlap on its own cases. We also propose a governance model with which the site keeps those errors independent over time. Health systems should then judge a clinical artificial intelligence (AI) tool by whether its failures overlap with their clinicians' failures, as well as by its accuracy.

title: AI-Mediated Employee Voice and Performance: Disentangling Informational and Affective Pathways
description:
arXiv:2610.25548v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Employee voice -- the discretionary expression of ideas, concerns, and suggestions intended to improve organizational functioning -- creates value inside firms, yet organizations increasingly replace or augment human-led listening with AI-enabled systems that collect, analyze, and route employee input at scale. Whether algorithmic listening replicates the value-creation mechanisms of human voice, and whether it alters the pathways through which voice translates into performance, remains an open question. This research proposal theorizes that traditional voice bundles two distinct functions, knowledge extraction and relational signaling, and that AI mediation may decouple them: strengthening the informational pathway (implemented improvement measures) while weakening the affective pathway (the experience of being heard). We propose a randomized field intervention at a global strategy consulting firm, covering approximately 2,000 client-facing consultants, that varies the form of listening across three conditions -- no structured voice, human-led survey-based voice, and AI-enabled conversational voice -- and links weekly team survey data to longitudinal performance ratings. A dual-mediation model is tested in which voice affects performance through (1) implemented process improvements and (2) affective well-being. The study extends voice theory to knowledge-intensive professional services, disentangles the micro-mechanisms of voice, and provides causal evidence on whether AI can serve as an effective listener.

title: Voice-Based AI Feedback in Higher Education: A Field Study on Quality and Actionability
description:
arXiv:2610.25560v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.

title: Causal Humility: Governing the Authority of Fairness Claims Under Causal Uncertainty
description:
arXiv:2610.25709v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems increasingly shape consequential decisions in employment, lending, healthcare, and public services, making fairness an important problem for auditing and governance. Fairness assessment often requires more than identifying disparities in outcomes; it also requires understanding how those disparities arise. Causal approaches to algorithmic fairness address this explanatory problem by representing pathways through which protected attributes and other factors may influence outcomes. Yet causal reasoning in sociotechnical systems remains uncertain: relevant confounders may be unobserved, causal directions contested, and conclusions sensitive to modeling assumptions and representational choices.
  We introduce causal humility as a governance framework for managing the relationship between epistemic uncertainty and causal authority. Drawing on causal fairness research, epistemology, political philosophy, and science and technology studies, causal humility has four requirements: making consequential assumptions and omissions visible; preserving contestability across defensible causal accounts; recognizing indeterminacy as a legitimate analytical outcome; and maintaining proportionality between evidentiary support and institutional authority or action.
  We operationalize these requirements through Causal Cards, a documentation artifact for recording the causal basis, assumptions, omissions, model dependence, and governance implications of fairness claims. Using the UCI Adult dataset as a worked epistemic demonstration, we show how different causal discovery procedures applied to the same observational data render fairness-relevant pathways visible, absent, or unresolved. Causal humility treats such disagreement as information about the limits of what can responsibly be claimed and the authority those claims should carry.

title: When Care Expands and Control Declines: Understanding Digital Privacy in End-of-Life Care
description:
arXiv:2610.25773v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Terminally ill patients generate extensive digital health data through hospital portals, physiological monitoring devices, consumer health applications, and end-of-life care platforms. Yet their ability to control this data is systematically undermined by the structural conditions of terminal care. Through semi-structured in-depth interviews with 21 terminally ill patients, 11 family caregivers, and 8 physicians recruited from tertiary hospitals, this study examines the digital privacy circumstances and subjective attitudes of patients in end-of-life contexts. Thematic analysis reveals five structural dimensions of digital privacy challenge: continuous bodily digitization without meaningful informed consent; cognitive decline driving involuntary proxy control of accounts; inferential data generation exceeding patients' epistemic boundaries; dissolution of individual privacy boundaries amid relational network restructuring; and the absence of institutional governance over post-mortem data. Patient privacy attitudes span three profiles: fundamental absence of privacy awareness, sustained active management under severe tool constraints, and perception of problems followed by resigned abandonment. Interviews with caregivers and physicians reveal benevolent substitution in the name of care needs, expansion of access beyond the initial task, and unresolved boundaries under absent institutional guidance. These findings reveal a compounding privacy vulnerability unique to end-of-life contexts and call for privacy-by-design principles, granular permission mechanisms, and institutional governance frameworks tailored to the needs of dying patients.

title: Exploring Visual Access and Proactive AI Tutoring for Handwritten Mathematics
description:
arXiv:2610.26411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Handwritten work captures mathematical reasoning that learners may not express in typed or voice-dictated messages. We built a multimodal AI tutoring platform in which a phone camera gives the tutor a live view of learners' work on paper. In a randomized online study, 117 adults solved calculus problems with Text-Reactive, Visual-Reactive, or Visual-Proactive assistance. Analysis of 2,140 tutor messages showed that visual access shifted assistance toward checking ongoing work, while proactivity enhanced error identification and directive hints. Learners valued feedback grounded in their writing; those who received proactive help rated it as supportive, and about a third wanted it more often. These findings inform when tutors should intervene and what they should address. We release the platform, prompts, and instruments, together with 255,984 timestamped images of handwritten work linked to tutoring conversations, intervention decisions, and learning outcomes, to support multimodal tutoring systems that preserve the affordances of handwritten work while providing adaptive feedback.

title: From TCP/IP to MCP: Security and Governance Lessons from Internet Protocols for Agentic AI
description:
arXiv:2610.26624v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The past two years have seen considerable interest in protocols for managing how AI agents interact with human users, external tools, and each other. In many ways, these protocols, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent2Agent (A2A), mirror the suite of protocols that underlie the modern internet. Motivated by this parallel, this paper draws lessons from the development, history, and governance of internet protocols with the aim of informing the responsible development of AI agent protocols. Based on our analysis, we make two conclusions. First, if AI agent protocols do not sufficiently prioritise security in the early stages of development, they risk accumulating a security deficit that becomes increasingly costly to address over time due to practical and economic challenges. Second, current governance structures for AI agent protocols centralise decision-making power in a small number of individuals and companies, raising important questions regarding legitimacy, especially if they become critical digital infrastructure. We conclude with a discussion and implications for policymakers and developers of AI agent protocols.

title: Reasoning-Aware Multicalibrated Reliability Predictors for Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.26645v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As people increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) for information, model providers need to communicate meaningful estimates of whether individual responses are correct or, more generally, reliable. In the context of hallucinations, existing work uses multicalibration to make such reliability predictions meaningful across application-relevant groups, such as prompt topics. Topic groups alone, however, can conceal systematic errors: within the same topic and confidence level, responses with different chain-of-thought (CoT) properties may exhibit opposing errors that cancel on average. In this work, we introduce reasoning-aware multicalibration, a framework that supplements application-relevant topic groups with groups derived from observable properties of CoT traces. We highlight that, theoretically, groupings based on CoT are "internally important", i.e., groupings for which the multicalibration guarantee is not societally crucial as it is for high-risk topics, but whose inclusion in the multicalibration procedure could easily and significantly improve predictive accuracy of the final reliability predictor. Empirically, we apply our framework to hallucination prediction and unsafe-response detection across a variety of benchmarks, and find that adding CoT groups to topic-based calibration reduces Brier score in both tasks. Interestingly, we find that multicalibrating with respect to CoT groups alone (without any topic information) already improves calibration across topics, suggesting that the predictor's errors depend on how the model reasoned, rather than what it was asked about in the prompt.

title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
description:
arXiv:2610.24035v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.

title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
description:
arXiv:2610.24168v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

title: Over reliant and underprepared: First responder resilience to disruption of operational technology
description:
arXiv:2610.24186v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The Emergency Services Sector (ESS) is responsible for taking life-saving action in the face of extreme crises. To enhance its response capabilities, the sector has spent the last two decades investing in new technology to improve their operational efficiency. This has created significant interdependencies and a culture among first responders of technical overreliance, raising questions about what would occur if those tools were suddenly disrupted. Several works have discussed the potential for terrorism to intentionally target ESS technology as part of a larger kinetic attack. Despite this, the resilience of first responder agencies to technological disruption and their preparedness for such an attack has largely remained unexplored. To bridge this gap, we implemented a novel scenario-based interview methodology involving senior officials from emergency service agencies across the United States. These interviews explored how each agency prepared for a disruption of operational technology and what factors might influence different levels of preparation between them. Participants were asked to describe their responses to a hypothetical scenario modeled after historical cyber-attacks against ESS infrastructure. The results indicate that while ESS agencies are prepared for short-term technological disruptions, they are likely to struggle with long-term or hybrid incidents. The data further revealed that agencies often lack dedicated expertise in cybersecurity, technology, and emergency management that could otherwise elevate resilience to interruptions of operational technology. These findings emphasize the need for investment in redundant analog systems, increased training for frontline personnel, and a focused effort against loss of specialized technical expertise among ESS agencies.

title: Usability, User Experience, and Acceptability of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality in Younger and Older Adults
description:
arXiv:2610.24237v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Immersive virtual reality (VR) adaptations of neuropsychological tests change how a test operates. Before their scores are interpreted, the individuals they are intended to assess should find them usable, acceptable and tolerable, and for older adults this evidence is usually missing. This study evaluated the experience of the Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), a head-gaze adaptation of the Trail Making Test that requires no hand-held controller, in 47 younger (20-38 years) and 44 older adults (64-81 years). After the task, participants rated usability, pragmatic and hedonic user experience, acceptability, and cybersickness. The study had three aims: to compare the two age groups on these ratings; to examine whether the ratings were associated with age group, gaming and technology experience, and whether cybersickness was associated with motion sickness susceptibility; and to examine whether the ratings were related to TMT-VR completion and error-adjusted times. Both groups rated the TMT-VR as highly usable, acceptable and pleasant to use. Older adults gave slightly lower usability and pragmatic ratings, but neither the age-group differences nor the associations with age group or previous experience were statistically significant after correction. Cybersickness was low, with 38 of the 91 participants reporting no symptoms; it did not differ between the age groups and was not associated with motion sickness susceptibility. No correlation between the ratings and TMT-VR performance survived correction. The TMT-VR with head-gaze selection is therefore usable, acceptable and well tolerated by older as well as younger adults. Because the ratings were favourable across the whole range of TMT-VR scores, slower or less accurate performance is unlikely to reflect difficulty with the interface.

title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
description:
arXiv:2610.24267v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 ONET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE). We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.

title: Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
description:
arXiv:2610.24269v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Digital-witnessing research explains how citizen testimony becomes publicly visible. Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.

title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
description:
arXiv:2610.24385v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. ID-TAP combines a query-conditioned neural utility model with a lightweight Bradley-Terry explorer, and transfers comparison evidence across related queries through similarity-weighted warm starts. The neural model shares statistical strength across queries while preserving query-specific scores, and efficient BT updates score hypothetical challengers. Across seven user-conditioned generation benchmarks under reference- and model-based preference simulators, ID-TAP achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated baselines within a fixed ten-round comparison budget. These results support information-directed challenger selection as an effective design for test-time persona adaptation.

title: YouTube Clips and Broad but Shallow Attention to Candidates: Evidence from the 2024 Tokyo Gubernatorial Election
description:
arXiv:2610.24387v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Video-sharing platforms and social media have gained influence in election campaigns, and third-party edited videos (called kirinuki in Japanese; hereafter, "clip videos") in particular have attracted attention. In Japan, Shinji Ishimaru, previously unknown nationally, finished second in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, a result widely attributed to his popularity on YouTube. Focusing on this case, we analyzed 44,331 YouTube videos relating to the nine leading candidates, posted between July 5, 2020, and July 7, 2024. Using cumulative views and engagement data as of June 25, 2025, we examined the relationship between clip videos and the attention candidates received. Regression analyses with standard errors clustered by channel showed that Ishimaru, the most watched candidate, did not draw the most active engagement. Videos mentioning Ishimaru received about 36% fewer likes and 41% fewer comments at the same number of views, whereas some candidates with fewer views recorded higher engagement rates. Clip videos were associated with this breadth of attention. They received about 1.8 times more views but 26% fewer comments at the same number of views, and mentions of Ishimaru were associated with about 2.6 times more views among non-clip videos. The interaction between the two, however, was not significant, and understanding the prominence of Ishimaru's cumulative views requires considering both the number of clip videos about him and the views per video. These results suggest that the spread of attention through clip videos may have functioned as a broad but shallow pathway, distinct from the formation of committed support.

title: Can AI agents make law? Evaluating AI legal relevance and creativity
description:
arXiv:2610.24661v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models, the artificial intelligence (AI) systems behind modern chatbots, are trained on vast amounts of legal text, but can they build on it to write law for situations that text never anticipated? In this study, we analyse AI agents' ability to draft a hypothetical "Constitution" for a "community of AI agents". We design "constitutional assemblies" in which a single language model plays several characters that debate to produce a draft constitution. We find that the assemblies converge on a robust floor of legal provisions, and generate a wide variety of different proposals around it, including several AI-specific provisions with no equivalent in human law. Looking more closely at the "creativity" of these AI agents, we find different levels: most proposals combine existing concepts and themes from human constitutions with AI-specific vocabulary. We introduce a measure of this recombination, which helps identify and highlight the most novel legal material. This study reveals a ceiling on AI creativity: the agents extend familiar legal ideas to new situations, but they do not work through what those situations would change. Although current AI models can help develop new laws, they still depend on human legal reasoning.

title: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives (Extended Version)
description:
arXiv:2610.24748v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.

title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
description:
arXiv:2610.24818v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.

title: The World as Viewed by 136 Countries: An Open, Curated, Annotated, and Multilingual Dataset of 118 Million State Media Articles
description:
arXiv:2610.24990v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: State media outlets often project their governments' narratives to target both domestic and foreign audiences. Because this content is plentiful and free to access, it appears widely in the web corpora that large language models (LLMs) are trained on and that retrieval systems draw from. However, the prevalence of state media in these corpora and its potential influence on LLM outputs remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce WorldStateMedia, an open dataset of 118 million state media articles from 136 countries in 114 languages. We extract these articles from existing pretraining corpora and annotate each outlet with level of state control from State Media Monitor. Using WorldStateMedia to audit these corpora, we find that, in English web crawls, the share of state media pages from editorially controlled (vs. independent) outlets rose from 39% in 2013 to 93% in 2025. In several low-resource languages, state media make up a substantial share of all web data, such as 17.8% for Uyghur and 7.8% for Belarusian. To characterize the differing narratives of news outlets, we compare Russian and Ukrainian state media in English and in their native languages, revealing asymmetric topical focus and opposing framings of contested issues such as Crimea. Furthermore, in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) experiment on territorial disputes, retrieving a country's state media shifts model answers toward that country's claims, most strongly for English-language (foreign-targeted) media. We release WorldStateMedia to support multilingual, cross-national insights on state media at https://huggingface.co/collections/manestay/worldstatemedia

title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
description:
arXiv:2610.25040v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.

title: Legal Guidance in the Wild: How Users Seek Legal Help in Real-World LLM Conversations
description:
arXiv:2610.25159v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: People ask conversational AI models about their legal rights, obligations, procedures, and personal situations that may have legal consequences. To study this behavior, we first need to distinguish requests for legal guidance from other legally themed discussions and unrelated conversations. We contribute a multi-axis taxonomy of legal queries capturing whether legal guidance is sought, how a request is formulated, and which legal domains it concerns; apply it to 2,122 naturally occurring WildChat-1M conversations; and create a human-reviewed gold evaluation set of 200 conversations. All annotations, model checkpoints, and evaluation code are publicly available. In this enriched sample, 71.1% of conversations containing legal content seek personalized or practical guidance. Rights-and-options advice is the most common primary request type among legal-content conversations, and 25.3% of guidance-positive conversations span multiple legal topics. The gold evaluation set supports a two-stage comparison of ModernBERT-base and ModernBERT-large against a TF-IDF cascade. Our framework supports large-scale studies of legal guidance in conversational AI, and the public release of the annotated data facilitates reproducible research and future model development.

title: Concept Representations in Vector Space: Toward an Interdisciplinary Study of Meaning Variation
description:
arXiv:2610.25184v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: An increasing number of disciplines recognize the explanatory potential of meaning-bearing mental structures through which individuals interpret the world and guide their behavior. Concept representations constitute a core class of these structures, emerging from individuals' experiences with concept referents and encoding and organizing their understanding of them. Recognizing a private level of meaning, where concepts are not objectively defined by rules in the world but constitute subjective structures in individuals' minds, raises a fundamental question: do different individuals actually mean the same thing when they invoke the same concept? As latent structures, concept representations are difficult to access and model empirically. The present study introduces a measurement framework that makes such representations empirically accessible through textual traces elicited under standardized conditions. Using transformer-based sentence embeddings, the framework maps standardized responses elicited for concepts into a high-dimensional shared vector space, opening concept representations to the systematic analysis of interindividual variation. It develops three analytical avenues: (1) comparing representational sharedness across concepts, (2) identifying variables that correlate with representational variation, and (3) examining how focal actors or subpopulations deviate from a reference population. Each avenue is illustrated through an empirical proof-of-concept drawing on a large-scale free-association dataset. Together, the demonstrations show how researchers from across disciplines can move from a research question and data source to analysis and interpretation. An accompanying GitHub repository provides a ready-to-use implementation of the framework for existing and custom datasets.

title: Aligning Language Models with Indigenous Community Cosmovision through Constitutional AI
description:
arXiv:2610.25298v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on corpora that reflect Western, anglophone worldviews. This asymmetry is not neutral: when a model answers questions about territory, community authority, or the relationship with nature, it does so from assumptions that may be alien to the communities using the system. This paper presents a system for aligning language models with the ethical principles of Indigenous communities in Latin America. Drawing on interviews with five Indigenous leaders and defenders, we built an operational cultural constitution grounded in an Indigenous cosmovision, with 12 principles. On this basis, we implemented a Constitutional AI (CAI) pipeline in two phases: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and direct preference optimization (DPO). The base models were Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. With only 24 preference pairs, improvements were modest but detectable in intergenerational transmission, linguistic caution, and consultation and consent. Qualitative analysis reveals that the SFT phase was responsible for the primary shift in alignment, while DPO refined specific categories. The system was deployed in a conversational interface with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that allows communities to feed the knowledge base, turning alignment into a participatory cycle. We argue the architecture is functional and will scale qualitatively once the corpus is expanded and computing constraints are resolved. The work constitutes a first iteration of an epistemic justice mechanism for value alignment in the Global South.

title: Selling in the Wild: Benchmark and Randomized Field Evidence for a Sales Agent Trained on Commercial Conversations
description:
arXiv:2610.25461v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We test whether Javo, a sales agent fine-tuned on 4.6 million consented, de-identified commercial conversations, sells better than a frontier general-purpose model and better than human sales associates. The evaluation has four parts. Study 1 scores the agent on two public sales benchmarks, SalesLLM and SmartSalesBench, against 10 frontier and open-weight models. Study 2 is a randomized controlled trial on 100 live websites in 14 industries (e-commerce, travel and hospitality, and high-consideration services), run from 1 May to 30 September 2026, in which 14.8 million visitors were randomized to no agent, Javo, or a frontier-model agent with an identical interface, catalog tools and guardrails. Study 3 isolates the effect of the model by comparing those two agent arms. Study 4 compares Javo with each site's own human associates on 20 sites with staffed live chat. Relative to no agent, Javo changed revenue per visitor by +10.0% (95% CI +5.1 to +14.9). Among engaged visitors, it changed conversion by +21.6% relative to the frontier-model agent (95% CI +16.9 to +26.3). Against human associates, its engaged conversion was 11.26% versus 11.20% (non-inferior, margin -7%, one-sided p = 0.004; no significant superiority), at 1.8% of the cost per conversation. Return rates, unsupported product claims and complaint rates met the prespecified safety guardrails.

title: Conditional information Retrieval for Longitudinal Survey Harmonisation
description:
arXiv:2610.26173v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Identifying conceptually equivalent questions across different surveys is a challenging information retrieval task where surface-level textual similarity is insufficient. Two questions may be lexically similar yet assess entirely different sociological sub-concepts, or lexically different yet conceptually equivalent. We introduce a conditional information retrieval framework that addresses this by decomposing the task into two steps: concept extraction, which identifies the underlying sociological concept of a survey question using a fine-tuned generative model, and concept-aware retrieval, which augments question representations with the extracted concept as an explicit conditioning signal for finer-grained alignment. To reflect the realistic data scarcity conditions of specialised social science annotation, we use CLOSER as a case study. Our framework consistently outperforms baselines by 2-3 points in both MAP and Recall. We further analyse fine-tuning strategies including SFT, DPO, and dynamic DPO, finding that SFT delivers the most stable gains while dynamic DPO interacts differently with instruction-tuned versus distilled reasoning backbones. Finally, we demonstrate that a model fine-tuned on a general social science thesaurus (ELSST) transfers robustly to task-specific survey data, offering a practical solution under data scarcity.
